title: Controlled Substance Schedule Overview
subtopic: Federal schedules and Massachusetts Schedule VI
learning_objectives: Separate federal controlled-substance status from Massachusetts scheduling consequences.
Identify the legal consequence that actually controls instead of reasoning from a schedule label alone.

orientation.text: Controlled-substance classification is a lookup rather than a judgement about how a drug behaves. Federal law collects the schedules established by section 202 of the Controlled Substances Act into 21 CFR Part 1308, one section per schedule: 1308.11 for Schedule I, 1308.12 for Schedule II, 1308.13 for Schedule III, 1308.14 for Schedule IV and 1308.15 for Schedule V. Each of those sections opens with the same sentence -- the schedule 'shall consist of the drugs and other substances, by whatever official name, common or usual name, chemical name, or brand name designated, listed in this section' -- and most of them go on to state that each drug or substance has been assigned the Controlled Substances Code Number set forth opposite it. Membership is therefore a matter of appearing on a list under some name, not of belonging to a pharmacologic family, which is why a drug-specific question has to be answered from the exact schedule provision rather than from an undifferentiated reference to Part 1308.

Massachusetts does not maintain a rival list. 105 CMR 700.002 establishes six schedules, and its first five subsections do nothing but point at the federal ones: 700.002(A) provides that Massachusetts Schedule I consists of the drugs and other substances, by whatever official name, common or usual name, chemical name, or brand name designated, listed in 21 CFR 1308.11, and (B) through (E) repeat that formula for 1308.12 through 1308.15 in turn. The consequence is worth stating plainly because it dissolves a whole class of imagined conflicts: for Schedules I through V there is no separate Massachusetts scheduling decision to look up. A drug's Massachusetts Schedule II status follows from its federal Schedule II listing, because the Massachusetts regulation adopted that listing instead of restating it. The sixth subsection is the one place where the two systems genuinely come apart.

105 CMR 700.002(F) provides that Schedule VI consists of all prescription drugs which are not included in any other schedule established by the Commissioner. It is a residual category defined by exclusion, so nothing about a drug's own pharmacology puts it there; a prescription drug reaches Schedule VI precisely because the federal lists that Massachusetts Schedules I through V incorporate do not reach it. That is what makes the label so easy to misread. 'Schedule VI' looks like a sixth and gentlest tier of controlled-substance regulation, when in substance it is the set of ordinary prescription medicines. Schedule VI status does not by itself make a drug federally controlled, and it does not by itself make the drug routinely MassPAT-reportable.

Two disciplines follow from that architecture. The first is to finish the classification properly: the schedule paragraphs in 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15 are typically prefaced 'Unless specifically excepted or unless listed in another schedule', and a number of the listings turn on quantity and formulation rather than on the active ingredient alone, so the thing being classified is the product in hand and not the molecule's reputation. The second is to treat the schedule as a premise. It identifies which body of dispensing, refill, transfer, partial-fill, record and reporting rules must now be opened; it does not itself answer any of those questions, in either sovereign. A candidate who stops at the label has done the lookup and skipped the rule.

comparison_tables.title: What a schedule label settles, and what it leaves open
columns: Settled by the schedule label alone?

cells: Is this drug on a federal controlled-substance list?
The particular section among 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15 that lists it, read with its own quantity and formulation limits

worked_examples.scenario: A prescriber sends an ordinary prescription for a maintenance medicine that appears nowhere in 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15. A student asks which Massachusetts schedule it sits in, and whether the pharmacy therefore owes the record and reporting duties that attach to controlled substances.
steps: Start with Massachusetts Schedules I through V. 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) define each of them as the drugs listed in the matching federal section, so a drug absent from 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15 is absent from Massachusetts Schedules I through V as well.

Ask the only question 105 CMR 700.002(F) then puts: is it a prescription drug? If it is, it falls into Schedule VI, which consists of all prescription drugs not included in any other schedule established by the Commissioner.
Stop before importing consequences. Schedule VI status does not itself make the drug federally controlled, and it does not itself make it routinely MassPAT-reportable.
Open the rule that governs the act the student is actually asking about, because the classification supplies the premise while the act-specific rule supplies the duty.
worked_examples.resolution: It is a Massachusetts Schedule VI drug, and nothing else follows automatically from that. The error the scenario invites is reading 'Schedule VI' as a sixth tier of controlled-substance regulation and importing federal controlled-substance duties that no federal listing ever imposed.

worked_examples.scenario: Two liquid preparations of the same narcotic active ingredient arrive on one order. The first contains 1.5 grams of codeine per 100 milliliters together with an active nonnarcotic ingredient in a recognized therapeutic amount. The second contains 150 milligrams of codeine per 100 milliliters together with a non-narcotic active medicinal ingredient. A colleague files both as Schedule II on the ground that codeine is a Schedule II drug.
steps: Test the colleague's premise. 21 CFR 1308.12(b)(1) does place codeine in Schedule II, but that paragraph is prefaced 'Unless specifically excepted or unless listed in another schedule', so the listing yields to a narrower placement.

Read the first preparation against 21 CFR 1308.13(e)(1)(ii), which covers not more than 1.8 grams of codeine per 100 milliliters with one or more active, nonnarcotic ingredients in recognized therapeutic amounts. At 1.5 grams per 100 milliliters the preparation is within that listing, so it is Schedule III.

Read the second against 21 CFR 1308.15(c)(1), which covers not more than 200 milligrams of codeine per 100 milliliters or per 100 grams in a preparation carrying non-narcotic active medicinal ingredients. At 150 milligrams per 100 milliliters it is within that listing.

Resolve the overlap the second preparation creates. Its strength also falls within the words of the Schedule III listing, and the preface decides between them: 21 CFR 1308.13(e) applies only 'unless specifically excepted or unless listed in another schedule', and the Schedule V paragraph lists it, so the narrower placement takes it.
Carry both answers into Massachusetts without a second lookup, because 105 CMR 700.002(C) and (E) consist of exactly the drugs listed in 21 CFR 1308.13 and 21 CFR 1308.15.
worked_examples.resolution: The two preparations are Schedule III and Schedule V respectively, and neither is Schedule II. The error is classifying the active ingredient instead of the product, which is exactly what the quantity thresholds and the 'unless listed in another schedule' preface exist to prevent.

worked_examples.scenario: A technician proposes a shortcut for the controlled-substance shelf: anything acting at an opioid receptor is a Schedule II narcotic and should be stored and recorded as one. You are asked to confirm the shortcut before the shelf is rearranged.
steps: Go to the provision rather than the class name. 21 CFR 1308.12(b)(1) places opium and opiate, and any salt, compound, derivative or preparation of opium or opiate, in Schedule II.

Read the rest of that sentence. It excludes a list of substances by name -- among them naloxone, naltrexone, nalmefene, nalbuphine, naloxegol, naldemedine, samidorphan, dextrorphan and apomorphine, together with their respective salts -- so the Schedule II opiate listing does not reach them at all.

Note precisely what that decides. It settles that the Schedule II opiate listing is not the source of any control over those substances; whether a given one of them is controlled elsewhere is answered only by reading 21 CFR 1308.11 and 1308.13 through 1308.15.

Apply the same reading to Massachusetts without a fresh lookup, because 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) consist of the drugs listed in those same federal sections, and a prescription drug they do not reach falls to Schedule VI under 105 CMR 700.002(F).
worked_examples.resolution: The shortcut is wrong and cannot be repaired, because the schedules list substances by name and several opioid-receptor drugs are named out of the Schedule II listing. The error is treating a pharmacologic class as though it were a classification, the same mistake as treating 'stimulant' as a schedule.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: 105 CMR 700.002(F) provides that Schedule VI consists of ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: all prescription drugs which are not included in any other schedule established by the Commissioner.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The federal schedules occupy 21 CFR ______ through ______, one section per schedule; Massachusetts states all of its schedules at 105 CMR ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 1308.11 through 1308.15; 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (F). Five federal schedules, six Massachusetts ones.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Why does a drug's Massachusetts Schedule II status follow from its federal listing without any separate state scheduling decision?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Because 105 CMR 700.002(B) defines Massachusetts Schedule II as the drugs and other substances listed in 21 CFR 1308.12, adopting the federal list rather than restating it, and 700.002(A) and (C) through (E) do the same for the other four schedules.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a drug in Massachusetts Schedule VI is federally controlled.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. Schedule VI is the residue of prescription drugs that the federal lists incorporated by 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) do not reach, and Schedule VI status does not itself establish federal controlled status.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: if a drug is reportable to MassPAT it must be federally scheduled.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. MassPAT reportability does not alter a drug's federal schedule, and Schedule VI status does not itself make a drug routinely MassPAT-reportable. The two questions are answered from different sources.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The schedule paragraphs of 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15 typically open with the same qualifier. Quote it, and say what work it does.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 'Unless specifically excepted or unless listed in another schedule.' It makes each listing yield to a specific exception and to a narrower placement elsewhere, which is how one active ingredient can sit in more than one schedule at different quantities.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: You have established that a drug is a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription drug and appears on no federal list. What have you still not answered?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Whatever the question actually asked. Classification is only the premise; the refill, transfer, partial-fill, record or reporting consequence comes from the rule governing that act.

quick_review.text: Federal controlled-substance schedules are defined in 21 CFR Part 1308 and drug-specific classification requires the applicable schedule provision.
Massachusetts Schedule VI captures prescription drugs not otherwise placed in Massachusetts Schedules I through V.
A Massachusetts Schedule VI label does not by itself establish federal controlled status or routine MassPAT reporting.

decision_logic.condition: A question asks whether a named drug is federally controlled.
decision_logic.action: Identify the drug's exact federal schedule provision before applying federal consequences.

decision_logic.condition: A prescription drug is not in Massachusetts Schedules I through V.
decision_logic.action: Evaluate it under Massachusetts Schedule VI and then apply the separate rule governing the requested act.

ma_vs_federal.text: Federal scheduling and Massachusetts Schedule VI answer different classification questions; neither label alone supplies every dispensing, transfer, or reporting consequence.

exceptions.text: A drug-specific or act-specific rule may add a narrower consequence, so classification is the start of the analysis rather than the final answer.

role_duties.duty: Confirm the controlling federal and Massachusetts classification before applying an act-specific rule.

common_traps.text: Treating every Massachusetts Schedule VI drug as federally controlled is incorrect.
Treating the schedule label as a complete answer to refill, transfer, or reporting questions skips the operative rule.
